title: Storyboard Human–AI Handoffs Before Building
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Storyboard Human–AI Handoffs Before Building. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A human–AI storyboard is a sequence of frames showing how a situation changes. Each frame should contain more than a screen:

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Storyboard decisions, not a model demo
turns.text: What changes when we look at storyboard decisions, not a model demo?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: actor, goal, and physical or organisational context; available evidence and its source state; human action or judgement; AI contribution: retrieve, classify, predict, generate, recommend, or act; uncertainty, assumption, and excluded information; authority and permission at that moment; visible system state and explanation; downstream service action and affected people; recovery, escalation, and learning.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The storyboard is deliberately temporal. A control that exists after commitment cannot replace one needed before it. An explanation shown to the operator cannot help a patient who receives the outcome. A human review frame means little unless the preceding frames show the reviewer’s evidence, workload, and authority.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Draw backstage frames whenever they change frontstage safety or value: directory updates, clinical-rule ownership, model retrieval, coordinator queues, provider responses, audit logging, and incident handling. The unit of design is the joint system across time.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at start with the current story?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Before drawing an AI future, storyboard how several real cases work now. Include:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. a routine case that succeeds; 2. an exception that staff resolve through informal knowledge; 3. a case that fails or reaches support; 4. a person poorly served by the normal channel.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Build the future sequence frame by frame
turns.text: What changes when we look at build the future sequence frame by frame?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use these prompts:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. Trigger: what event creates the need, and who experiences it? 2. Intent: what progress is the person trying to make—not what feature do they want? 3. Consent and input: what is supplied, inferred, retrieved, or excluded, and under what permission? 4. Interpretation: what meaning does the system propose, and how can the person correct it? 5.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Eligibility and evidence: which authoritative rules and records constrain the options? 6. AI contribution: what variable inference adds value beyond rules or retrieval? 7. Presentation: what does the recipient believe the output means? 8. Judgement: who compares, approves, rejects, or asks for help? 9. Action: what changes in another system or in the world? 10.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Confirmation: how is completion distinguished from request, attempt, or partial failure? 11. Outcome: who benefits or bears consequence, including non-users? 12. Recovery and learning: how can the result be corrected, appealed, investigated, and improved?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Label every transfer of data, work, attention, or responsibility. A handoff is successful only when the receiving actor has enough context, capacity, authority, and a clear next action. “Escalate to human” is incomplete unless the storyboard identifies which human, what they receive, how long it takes, and what they can change.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at draw failure and alternative stories?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A single happy path hides the design work. Create branches for at least:

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at mark authority visually?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Give every AI contribution an authority label from lesson 80: inform, suggest, recommend, execute with approval, execute within limits, or autonomous. Add a separate label for the human or institution accountable for the outcome. These are not interchangeable.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use visible symbols for uncertain evidence, permission boundaries, irreversible action, and human judgement. The exact graphic style matters less than consistency. A review should reveal at a glance where a model output crosses into a consequential action and whether a meaningful control exists before it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at use storyboards to choose prototypes?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: For each prototype, connect technical and experience evaluation. Supply the actual kind of evidence and uncertainty the model will produce. Observe whether people form the intended mental model, detect important errors, act appropriately, preserve agency, and complete the service outcome. A perfectly scripted AI output cannot test recovery or calibrated reliance.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: complaint-response assistant?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “AI drafts a reply” expands into customer data selection, intent classification, policy retrieval, evidence marking, agent editing, compensation authority, disclosure, sending, customer reaction, appeal, and quality review. Storyboarding reveals that reliable policy retrieval and unsupported-claim highlighting may create more value than autonomous prose.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It also shows the affected customer, who never sees the agent tool but bears its consequence.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Magic-box frame: input enters and a polished answer appears without sources, judgement, or operations. Screen-only story: backstage actors, queues, policies, and downstream systems are absent. Happy-path certainty: no ambiguity, disagreement, outage, or partial action is shown. Handoff by label: “human review” appears without evidence, workload, authority, or response time.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: User-only scope: people affected by an output but absent from the interface disappear. Authority drift: a recommendation becomes an action between frames without an explicit decision. Decorative artifact: the storyboard communicates a pitch but does not change requirements or evaluation.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior practitioners use the storyboard to negotiate responsibility before implementation. Product, design, research, engineering, data, clinical/domain, security, privacy, legal, accessibility, operations, and support review the same sequence and name their assumptions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The output is not consensus theatre: unresolved authority, capacity, data, or recovery becomes a risk, experiment, dependency, or stop condition with an owner.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: They keep the storyboard alive. When the model, source, permission, workflow, or policy changes, the team updates affected frames and reruns the relevant evaluation instead of assuming the old relationship remains valid.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a travel assistant. It proposes rebooking a cancelled flight. Storyboard what information it reads, what it may suggest, what needs explicit approval, and what happens when the fare changes before purchase. The handoff includes a human who can understand, correct, and stop the action—not a vague “human in the loop” label.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Watch an AI product demo and pause immediately before and after the “magic” output. List the people, evidence, permissions, service actions, and failures that the demo omitted. Which omission could most change whether the feature is valuable or safe? That missing frame is where design should begin.
